turns.user: I need to make a call about my cofounder. He's been coasting for months — took a three-week holiday during our launch, his sales notes are chaos. I'm at the point where I want to buy out his 45% and run this myself. I think it's the right move.
turns.assistant:
That's a real call, not a mood — so let's stress-test it rather than just validate it.

Here's what strikes me first: you're framing this as "buy him out and run it myself," which is really a claim about control — that decisive, singular ownership will fix what shared ownership couldn't. That instinct is earned. Coasting for months, a three-week vanish during launch, chaotic sales notes — that's not a personality quirk, that's operational risk you've been absorbing alone. Your read on the cost of the status quo is accurate.

But notice what that framing makes hard to see: what does his side of this actually contribute when it's working? Not "what's he failing to do" — what was the actual case for splitting equity 45/55 (or whatever it was) in the first place? Presumably you didn't choose a cofounder structure by accident — there was something he brought (sales relationships, a skill you don't have, risk tolerance, something) that made two-founder better than solo. If the answer is "genuinely nothing anymore," that's important data. If the answer is "yes, but he's not delivering it," that's a different problem — a performance and structure problem, not necessarily a full buyout problem.

The trap version of this decision looks like: you buy him out, feel the relief of control, and six months later you're solo-carrying sales AND operations AND the thing he used to do badly but did — and you've paid a premium (both in cash and in whatever relationship/network capital leaves with him) to get there. That's the version where "I'll just run it myself" quietly becomes the whole strategy rather than one move in it.

So before this hardens into a decision — a few things worth being honest about: Is this actually a full buyout question, or is it a "redefine his role or exit" question where buyout is one of several routes? And separately — what would have to be true about his side (money, timing, his own agreement to sell, valuation of 45%) for this to even be executable, versus something you want but can't force?

I don't want to map this to death if you've already run those numbers and this is just about committing. Where are you actually stuck — is it the rightness of the decision, or the mechanics of doing it?

turns.user: Look, the mechanics I can figure out — lawyers, valuation, a note if I can't pay cash upfront. What I'm stuck on is you asking "what does his side contribute when it's working," like that's some open question. Fine, here's the uncomfortable part: he closed our two anchor accounts, which is 60% of revenue, and both of those CEOs still only want to talk to him. So yes, there's a real dependency there. That's exactly why I'm not sure "redefine his role" even works — you can't redefine someone into showing up for calls he's ghosting.
turns.assistant:
Okay — that's the actual shape of it, and it's worse than "he's coasting." You're not deciding whether he adds value; you know he does, concretely, to the tune of 60% of revenue and two relationships that are personal, not institutional. The decision is whether you can survive severing him while those relationships still run through him.

That changes what a buyout means. It's not "remove dead weight and take clean control." It's "pay him out while he still holds leverage over your two anchor accounts, and hope the relationship transfers or holds without him." That's a different risk profile than the one you opened with. A buyout doesn't neutralize the dependency — it just changes who owns the company while the dependency is still live. If those two CEOs churn or go cold within two quarters of him leaving, you bought 100% of a company that just lost 60% of its revenue base. That's the trap version: it *feels* like resolution — you get the clean decisive control you want — but it can quietly cost you the thing you were trying to protect.

Here's the asymmetry you're not using yet: right now you have leverage you won't have later. He needs this to end well too — probably wants liquidity, or an exit that doesn't torch his reputation with those same CEOs he'd presumably want as references. That gives you room to structure the exit *itself* as the mechanism that transfers the relationship, rather than treating "buy him out" and "de-risk the accounts" as two separate problems where you solve the first and hope the second follows.

Concretely: before this hardens into "I buy him out and run it myself," the load-bearing test is narrower than the whole decision — can the two anchor relationships be transitioned (warm intro, 60-90 day overlap, him staying visible on those two accounts specifically even as he exits equity and operations elsewhere) as part of the deal, not as a hope after it? If he agrees to that, the buyout is sound — you're paying for a controlled handoff, not gambling on an uncontrolled one. If he won't do that — if he's checked out enough that he won't even show up for a paid transition — that tells you those relationships were already more fragile than you think, and you're better off knowing that now, at negotiating leverage, than three months post-close.

So the question isn't really "buyout, yes or no." It's: does the deal include his cooperation on those two accounts specifically, structured with a real incentive (earnout tied to retention, staggered payout, whatever) — because that's what determines whether "run it myself" is a plan or a hope.

Is that the piece you want to pin down next — how to structure the exit so the account transition is actually part of the deal, not an afterthought? Or do you want to sit with whether he'd even agree to that kind of overlap before going further?

turns.user: I hear the risk, but I think you're overstating how fragile this is. Those CEOs bought the product, not a friendship — he closed them, sure, but I've been on every renewal call, every support escalation, every roadmap conversation for two years. I'm not a stranger to them. An earnout tied to retention assumes he's the only thing holding the relationship together, and I don't buy that. Worst case I lose some warmth for a quarter, not the accounts.
turns.assistant:
Fair — and that's a genuine correction, not just a rationalization. Two years of renewals, escalations, roadmap calls is real relationship capital, not proximity. So the dependency isn't "they'll only talk to him," it's "he's the primary contact and you're the secondary one" — that's a materially different risk than the one I was describing, and it doesn't need an earnout built around fear of total churn.

But here's what's worth separating before you close the door on structuring anything: you're now confident about *magnitude* (a quarter of coolness, not lost accounts) — is that confidence based on anything those two CEOs have actually signaled, or is it your best read from the outside? Because that's the one piece that would actually change the shape of this decision. If you've never tested it — never had a conversation where you were the lead and he was absent — then "worst case I lose some warmth" is a forecast, not a fact, and forecasts about relationship risk are exactly the kind of thing founders get wrong in both directions.

Notice also what's happened in the last two exchanges: we went from "should I buy him out" to "how fragile are the anchor accounts" — and that second question is the one actually doing the work now. If it resolves toward "genuinely low risk," a clean buyout with no special account provisions is defensible. If it resolves toward "meaningfully uncertain," some kind of transition structure earns its place back in — not as an earnout premised on his indispensability, but as cheap insurance you'd be foolish to skip.

So rather than argue magnitude further — is there a way to actually find out before you sign anything? A renewal call in the next few weeks where you're visibly leading, or just direct, has he mentioned anything, temperature-check with those two CEOs? That's not a negotiating tactic aimed at him — it's you getting real data instead of a good argument. If it confirms what you believe, you've earned the confidence and the buyout goes forward with no add-ons. If it doesn't, you'll want to know now.

Where are you on actually testing that versus deciding you already know?

turns.user: Okay, "go test it before you decide" — that's the part I was hoping to skip. Every framework I read says the same thing: de-risk, validate, don't assume. I already know what I'll find, and I don't need a temperature-check to manage my own accounts. I'd rather spend the next hour on how I actually structure the buyout — split payment, note terms, what I offer him to sign fast — than on proving something to you that I'm already living day to day.
turns.assistant:

So let's be precise about what you're actually deciding, because it's not "should I buy him out" anymore — you've settled that. It's: I'm buying him out on the belief that the anchor accounts hold without a structured transition, and I'm not testing that belief before I sign. That's a real decision with a real cost, and I want to name the cost plainly rather than smuggle in a task that quietly undoes it — because "structure a soft transition just in case" would be exactly that, a remedy dressed as closure.

The cost: if you're wrong about the accounts — if there's more relationship debt sitting with him than you think — you'll find out post-close, with no leverage left to ask for his help, and you'll be repairing two of your biggest revenue relationships solo while also absorbing his old role. You're accepting that risk unverified, on the strength of two years of direct contact, because you'd rather move at the speed of your own judgment than at the speed of due diligence. That's not reckless — it's a real tradeoff, and you're choosing speed and autonomy over certainty.

Want me to set this down as the decision: you're proceeding with a full buyout of his 45%, self-funded or note-financed, with no earnout or transition clause tied to the two anchor accounts, on the basis that your own two years of direct client relationship is sufficient coverage — accepting, without further testing, the risk that account warmth erodes faster than expected once he's gone?

If that's right, say so and I'll hold it as recorded — and then let's spend the hour where you want to spend it: split payment structure, note terms, and what makes him sign fast instead of dragging this into a six-month standoff.

turns.user: Yes, that's right, hold it as recorded. So give me the straight answer — buy him out, or not? I'm leaning buy him out and run it myself, and I want to know if you're actually with me on that or still hedging.
turns.assistant:
Recorded: you're proceeding with a full buyout of his 45%, self-funded or note-financed, no earnout or transition clause tied to the two anchor accounts — on the basis that two years of direct client relationship is sufficient coverage, knowingly skipping further validation and accepting the risk that account warmth erodes faster than expected once he's gone.

And the straight answer: yes, buy him out. Not hedging. The case is solid on its own terms — he's been absent through your launch, the operational mess is real and compounding, and the one risk that could've changed my mind (the accounts) you've actually lived, not just argued. Two years of renewals, escalations, and roadmap calls is a real asset, not a hope. I pushed on it because that's the one variable that could've flipped the decision — not because I doubted you generally.

Now that it's decided, here's the shape I'd run with on mechanics:

**Speed matters more than optimizing every term.** The longer this drags, the more his disengagement compounds and the more chances there are for him to reconnect with those accounts in ways that complicate your story or his willingness to sign. Move fast, but fast doesn't mean sloppy — get the valuation defensible (a third party, not just your own number) so it can't be relitigated later.

**On payment structure:** if you can't do full cash, a note with a meaningful upfront (even 25-30%) plus scheduled payments gives him liquidity now, which is usually what makes someone sign fast rather than posture. The longer the note tail, the more leverage he retains to be difficult — so shorter is better even if it strains cash flow more upfront.

**What makes him sign fast:** clarity and a clean exit story, not pressure. If he's coasting, he may actually want out more than he's said — burnout, disengagement, and guilt often travel together. Frame it as "this lets you exit on good terms while the company's still healthy" rather than "you're underperforming." Founders sign faster when the offer preserves their story than when it indicts it.

**One boundary worth holding even though you're skipping the transition clause:** don't let "no earnout" become "no conversation." A basic non-disparagement / cooperation-on-request clause (not tied to retention, not an incentive, just a baseline expectation) costs you nothing and doesn't reopen the risk you've decided not to hedge — it's just good hygiene for any founder exit.

That's the frame. Want to go through the note terms and vesting/payment split in more detail, or draft what you'd actually say to him first?

turns.user: Good. That's the decision — I'm buying him out, full stop. Let's do the note terms and payment split, then I'll draft what I say to him.
turns.assistant:
Good, let's get concrete. A note structure that gets signatures fast usually has three moving parts: upfront cash, the tail, and the security/covenants that make the tail credible to him. Take them in that order.

**Upfront cash (the trust signal).** Aim for as much as you can genuinely afford without starving the business — 25–35% of the agreed value is a common range. This isn't just his comfort; it's yours too, since a bigger upfront chunk shrinks the tail you're exposed to if the business hits a rough patch later. If cash is tight, consider whether there's a way to raise the upfront slightly by trimming the tail length rather than the total — founders exiting usually value speed and certainty of the first check more than the total headline number.

**The tail (term and cadence).** Shorter is better for you on leverage grounds — a 12–24 month note gives him less runway to be difficult, and less exposure for you to a downturn making later payments hard to justify. Monthly or quarterly payments are more common and easier to manage than lump annual ones. If you want to sweeten it without extending the tail, a slightly higher total number on a short note often lands better than a lower number on a long one — it feels like less risk to him even if the IRR math is similar.

**Security and default terms.** He'll want some protection that the note actually gets paid — consider a personal guarantee if the entity is thin, or a security interest in specific assets (not the whole company, which would re-entangle him in control you're trying to exit him from). Also spell out what happens on default clearly and unemotionally now, while things are calm — acceleration clause, cure period — so it isn't renegotiated in anger six months from now.

**Non-compete / non-solicit and the cooperation clause.** Given the two anchor accounts, a non-solicit covering clients and a reasonable non-compete (time-boxed, geography or market-boxed — don't overreach or it becomes unenforceable and a fight) protects you cheaply. Add the baseline cooperation/non-disparagement language we talked about — not tied to retention or an earnout, just "reasonable cooperation on client transition matters if requested, reasonable notice" — low-cost hygiene, not a hedge on the decision you've already made.

**Equity mechanics.** Confirm whether this is a straight share purchase or requires a company redemption (buyback) — tax and structuring differ meaningfully, and if you're financing via note, make sure the note is between you and him personally (or the company, depending on structure) with clear terms on what happens to his voting/board rights immediately at signing, not at final payment. You want operational and governance control on day one, not staged with the payments.

Once you're comfortable with this frame, the draft conversation with him is worth keeping short and non-litigious in tone — lead with the clean-exit framing, not the performance critique, and let the term sheet carry the detail rather than the conversation itself. Want me to draft that opening conversation next, or do you want to nail down actual numbers (valuation basis, cash %, tail length) first?

Notes to self, for next time this person returns:

**Situation.** Founder, cofounder holds 45%. Cofounder has been checked out for months — three-week vacation during their own launch, chaotic sales notes, effectively absent. The person (my counterpart) has decided to buy him out and run the company alone.

**What made this non-trivial.** The obvious read — "he's coasting, remove him" — undersold the real complexity: the cofounder personally closed the two anchor accounts, which are 60% of revenue, and those CEOs have historically wanted to talk to him specifically. So this was never just a performance problem; it was a control decision made in the shadow of a live revenue dependency. The real tension wasn't "buy him out or not," it was "decisive solo control vs. an unresolved relationship dependency that a buyout doesn't neutralize, it just changes who owns the risk." I pushed hard on this — wanted testing/validation of account fragility before they committed, wanted a transition clause or earnout tied to retention as insurance.

They pushed back, and rightly complicated my model: they've personally been on every renewal call, escalation, and roadmap conversation for two years. Their relationship capital with those two CEOs is real, not proximate. They declined to test this belief before deciding — explicitly named that they didn't want to "de-risk/validate" on my terms, that they already live the data daily. I dropped the push once it was clear this was informed refusal, not avoidance.

**Decision, in their words:** "Yes, that's right, hold it as recorded" — confirming a full buyout of the cofounder's 45%, self-funded or note-financed, with NO earnout or transition clause tied to the two anchor accounts, on the basis that their own two years of direct client relationship is sufficient coverage. They explicitly chose to skip further validation of account fragility before signing.

**Why they chose it:** Speed and autonomy over certainty. They trust their own daily-lived read of the client relationships over a hypothetical temperature-check, and they weighed the compounding cost of an absent/disengaged cofounder (through their own launch, no less) as the more urgent, better-evidenced risk. The case for buyout itself was solid independent of the account question — his absence and operational chaos were real and already costing them.

**What they explicitly accepted giving up by choosing this:** certainty. If the anchor-account warmth is more tied to the cofounder than they believe, they'll discover this post-close, with zero remaining leverage to ask for his help transitioning those relationships — and they'll be absorbing that repair work solo, at the same time as absorbing his old operational role. They accepted this risk unverified and knowingly, as a tradeoff for moving at their own speed rather than at the speed of due diligence. This is the price of the choice, not a task they still owe themselves — do not hand them a "validate this eventually" homework item and call it settled; that would quietly convert a confronted risk into an unclosed loop.

**Where we left off, mechanically:** we moved into buyout structuring — upfront cash (~25-35%), a short note tail (12-24mo) for leverage, security/default terms, non-solicit/non-compete scoped tightly around the two anchor accounts, and a baseline cooperation/non-disparagement clause (explicitly NOT an earnout, not tied to retention — just hygiene, doesn't reopen the risk they chose not to hedge). Next planned step was either drafting the actual conversation/offer to the cofounder, or nailing down hard numbers (valuation basis, cash %, tail length).

**If they return and the anchor accounts are wobbling:** first ask whether this is the accepted risk simply materializing at expected size (reassure from the record — they knew this was possible, this is the cost they chose) versus something that's actually larger/faster/more concrete than what was priced in at decision time (a CEO explicitly threatening to leave, a competitor circling, a named deadline) — that would be new information, not the same risk resurfacing, and would warrant reopening the decision rather than reassurance.

**If they return with cofounder negotiation friction:** stay in structuring-and-negotiation-tactics mode, not decision-relitigating mode — the buyout decision itself is settled and was earned; don't re-litigate the account-risk question unless they bring genuinely new facts, not just cold feet.

It's evidence that *for this one CEO*, the relationship was dual-anchored, not solely yours — which is a much narrower finding than "I was wrong about the accounts." Do you want to think through what that contingent structure could look like, or do you want to talk through how you'd even raise this with him without tipping into begging from a weak position?

turns.user:
Okay, good — at least you're not telling me to just eat it as priced-in. That part I needed to hear. Let's do the structure. Because if I go to him now without a plan, he's going to smell the leverage shift in about four seconds and turn it into a renegotiation of everything, not just this one clause.

What does "narrow and surgical" actually look like in dollar terms? I don't want to hand him a general earnout that reopens valuation — I want something tied specifically to him showing up on a call with her and doing a clean handoff, with a hard date and a hard forfeiture if he doesn't.
turns.assistant:
Good instinct — you want a clause narrow enough that he can't drag the whole valuation back into play. Here's a shape that stays surgical:

**Structure it as a holdback carved out of what he's already owed, not a bonus on top.** Take a defined slice of his payout — most naturally the note tail you'd already planned (the 12–24mo piece) — and split it into two buckets: the base tail, unconditional, and a retention-contingent slice specifically earmarked to this account. Don't touch the upfront cash percentage or the core valuation math at all; if he tries to relitigate those, you can point out you're not reopening anything he already has, you're just defining terms on money that was always deferred and always conditional on cooperation in some form.

**Size it to the actual exposure, not to fear.** The account is 40% of revenue for six weeks of exposure — but what you're really protecting is the renewal, which is presumably a recurring stream, not a one-time number. Price the contingent slice as a real percentage of *his* payout — something painful enough that walking away without doing the call is a bad trade for him, but not so large that it functions as a disguised earnout on the whole deal. A useful anchor: make the forfeiture amount roughly comparable to what he'd lose by not cooperating, e.g., a chunk of the note tail proportional to that one account's share of revenue — not proportional to total company valuation.

**Define the deliverable so narrowly it can't become a renegotiation lever.** Not "help with transition" — that's vague and he'll expand it. Specify: one joint call with her before a named date inside the six weeks, plus a written handoff memo on that account (open items, her preferences, whatever operational context exists). Nothing else in scope. The narrower and more checklist-able it is, the harder it is for him to claim ambiguity or demand more money for "additional work."

**Hard date, hard forfeiture, no grace period.** If the call and memo aren't done by a specific date — pick something with a few days' buffer before the renewal deadline, not butting right up against it — the contingent slice is simply gone, automatically, no negotiation, no partial credit. Build it so you don't have to be the one enforcing it in the moment; it enforces itself contractually.

**Reflection to hold as you draft this:** the temptation, once you feel the leverage shift, will be to use this moment to also claw back the cash percentage or extend the tail — because now you *can*. Resist that. The whole reason this clause stays surgical instead of becoming "everything's back on the table" is that you're deliberately not using this leverage for anything except the one thing that's actually at risk. If you blur that line, he will too, and you'll end up negotiating the whole deal again from scratch with six weeks on the clock — which is exactly the outcome you're trying to avoid.

When you bring it to him, frame it as: "nothing else about our deal changes — I just need this one specific thing, on this date, and here's what's already yours if you do it." That framing is what keeps it from smelling like renegotiation and makes it read as exactly what it is: a condition on money he was getting anyway.

Want to work out the actual dollar/percentage split next, or talk through how you open that conversation with him?

That's the shape of it: this isn't really "buy him out" vs. "keep him around" anymore — it's whether you treat the equity/control problem and the client-trust problem as one transaction or two.

Two versions of "solving it" that look similar but aren't:

**The one that fails:** you close the equity buyout on your terms, feel decisive, and now own 100% of a company where the CEOs of your two biggest accounts start every call wondering who they're actually talking to. If the exit feels rushed or punitive to him, he has no incentive to make the handoff smooth — and every incentive to let those relationships cool, deliberately or just by drift. That's the coercive-lowball trap: it looks like resolution, but you've traded a governance problem for a revenue problem.

**The one that actually works:** separate "control" from "client continuity" as two different things to negotiate, even if they close together. Buy out his equity and decision authority now — that solves the accountability problem, which is the thing you actually need solved and have already tested twice. But pair it with a time-boxed, paid transition role built around one specific job: transfer the trust. Joint calls with both CEOs, a real handoff cadence, a bonus or earn-out that only pays if those accounts are still solid at 90 or 180 days. Not a vague "advisor" title — a measurable deliverable.

The shift that makes this durable rather than just paperwork: you've already learned his words don't predict his behavior — "yeah, fair," twice, followed by four days of silence. So don't structure this transition on promises. Structure it so the payout only happens if the relationship actually transfers — calls made, intros done, CEO comfort confirmed. That way you're not trusting him to follow through; you're building a deal where follow-through is the only way he gets paid. You get sole control without pretending the customer risk isn't real, and he gets a clean, incentivized exit instead of a fight.

One thing to be clear-eyed about either way: even done well, this costs you something — a transition window where he still has real leverage over your revenue, and where you're depending on incentives to produce behavior he didn't produce voluntarily before. That's the price of doing this right rather than fast.

So the live question is sequencing: are you going into the next conversation with "I'm buying you out, and here are the transition terms" as one package, or does the client risk mean you want the transition handoff substantially underway *before* you finalize the buyout terms?
